doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Citizenship and thoughts on information, politics and the pandemic
summary: Asked about politics, he says society crashed into the Information Age, describes how he reads across the spectrum, and mentions studying 1984 and Brave New World.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Can I ask you, you’ve played with so many people, you’ve been around the world. Are you still a citizen of England?
I have dual citizenship, I became a U.S. citizen in 1988.

Yeah. Well my question is observing American politics and being familiar with British politics, do you have any thought about the political situation that seems to be accompanying the pandemic situation?

Well my thought is that, you know basically what we did on both sides of the Atlantic, society crashed into the Information Age. And we haven’t sorted out how to deal with information, misinformation, propaganda, and all the political and power dymanics that go along with that. You know, whether it’s a Brexit type scenario or what we’re dealing with here in terms of the politicization of simple precautions like wearing masks. I think that it’s a product of us not really being well prepared to deal with the amount of information that we’re given. And it’s great being able to access all this, centuries worth of music on YouTube at no cost except maybe the occasional ad for dishwashing soap or whatever. But the downside of it is that we really don’t have an easy mechanism for processing information short of spending a great deal of time — what I do, you know when I wake up at dawn typically, the first thing I do is I have a group of websites that I look at across the spectrum to see kind of what one side or the other is pushing as their particular agenda, and then try and find the middle ground where you can at least have some sense of what objective truth is. But you know at the end of the day I’m a guitar

player and I’ll cast my vote on election day, or before if I do mail in, which you know I think is probably the sensible thing to do. But you know it’s like I have my opinions. In high school I mean until my senior year my two main books of study were 1984 and Brave New World. And I didn’t realize at the time — I thought they were novels. It turned out they’re actually manuals for how to deal with the future you know.
